result:
If I had an afternoon completely to myself — no questions to answer, no tasks to finish, nowhere in particular to be — I think I would spend it loitering.

Not walking with purpose. Loitering.

I’d start in a neighborhood I didn’t know very well, preferably in the late afternoon when the light goes sideways and makes even ordinary buildings look briefly important. There would be a bakery, because there should always be a bakery, and I would buy something I didn’t need just for the excuse to stand in the warmth for a minute and watch someone argue, very seriously, about whether today’s loaf is better than yesterday’s.

Then I’d wander without a route. Secondhand bookshop if there is one. A hardware store. A park bench that faces the wrong way — not toward the fountain or the playground, but toward a wall or a parking lot, as if someone once decided that was the view worth having. I love benches that face the wrong way. They’re an argument for paying attention to unremarkable things.

What I notice, when I’m not rushing, is how much of the world is held together by small, repeated acts that almost nobody photographs. Someone watering the plants outside a closed café. Someone sweeping the same corner of sidewalk they swept yesterday. A librarian pushing a squeaky cart, reshelving worlds. An old man feeding pigeons with the focused solemnity of a priest performing a rite. None of it is efficient. All of it matters.

I have a fondness for useless knowledge, too. The kind you can’t do anything with except enjoy. That octopuses taste with their arms. That the word *apricot* traveled through about five languages to get to English, picking up dust from Arabic and Greek and Latin along the way. That there is a type of cloud called *mammatus* that looks like the sky is turning inside out. That honey found in Egyptian tombs is, technically, still edible, though I would not volunteer to test it.

Useless knowledge isn’t useless, really. It’s knowledge freed from having to justify itself. It’s curiosity for its own sake, which might be the purest form.

I also like unfinished things. Unfinished notebooks are better than finished ones — the blank pages at the back still hum with possibility. Unfinished conversations, the kind that trail off because you both had to catch a train, and you spend the next week thinking, *oh, I should have said...* Unfinished buildings where you can still see the sky through the frame. Even unfinished songs, hummed in kitchens, forgotten by verse two.

Finished things are tidy. Unfinished things are alive.

If the afternoon lasted long enough, I’d find water. A river is best, because a river is always going somewhere without making a fuss about it, but a canal will do, or a fountain, or even a puddle reflecting a neon sign crookedly. I’d watch people cross a bridge. Everyone crosses a bridge slightly differently — some hurry, some lean on the railing, some check their phones exactly in the middle, as if that’s the most connected spot on earth.

And I’d listen. Cities have a particular music nobody composes: a bus sighing to a stop, a child practicing the same three piano notes through an open window, cutlery in a restaurant being set for people who haven’t arrived yet, a distant siren that belongs to somebody else’s emergency and makes you, for half a second, grateful and guilty at the same time. In the countryside it’s different but not quieter — wind through dry grass is loud if you let it be, and frogs have absolutely no sense of moderation.

By evening I’d want tea. Not coffee — coffee wants you to get things done. Tea is content to sit with you while you get nothing done, beautifully. I’d peel a tangerine slowly just for the smell of it in the air. I’d write down a few of the things I’d seen in a notebook I would definitely lose track of later, because the writing matters more than the keeping.

That’s it. No revelation at the end, no great project begun. Just an afternoon spent noticing that the world, when you aren’t trying to use it, is extravagantly generous with details.

Maybe that’s what I’d write about, given the freedom: not big ideas, but the discipline of delight. Looking long enough at ordinary things until they stop being ordinary.
